Precise RX

Product and company names have been changed due to an NDA.

Precise RX is an AI-assisted analysis platform for clinical trials. Lab teams describe what they need in a chat, and an AI agent merges, checks and cleans trial data, writes and runs the R code, and turns the results into reports.

My role

From a blank page to a pilot

As Senior UX/UI Designer, I worked on Precise RX for a year and a half, building the web platform from scratch with a second designer, a PM and the CTO. Every week the client joined a call and described the features they wanted. We split the features between the two designers. I turned mine into concrete flows, presented them to the team, and then we showed every update to the client on the next weekly call.

Challenge

Replacing a legacy tool with a conversation

Before Precise RX, lab teams ran trial analyses in a dated, hard-to-use legacy tool. Data from separate files (drug concentrations, dosing, demographics) had to be merged, checked and cleaned by hand before any analysis could start, and reports were assembled without any AI help.

  1. 01

    A complex domain

    Pharmacokinetic analysis has many steps, many files and a lot of code. The interface had to keep all of that understandable for people who are scientists, not developers.

  2. 02

    Ideas without sketches

    New features usually arrived as a description on a client call. I had to turn those words into concrete interfaces while keeping a growing product consistent.

Deep dive 01

Analysis as a conversation with an AI agent

The client described the idea in words: an AI agent that takes a scientist from raw trial files to a finished analysis. I designed how that conversation looks and behaves.

  1. 01

    Always know where you are

    A trial analysis follows a fixed path: Data Merging, Anomalous Data Detection, Data Cleaning, Analysis. In a long chat that path gets lost, so I pulled it out into a stepper at the top. It works like breadcrumbs: whatever the agent is doing, the current stage stays in view.

  2. 02

    Nothing runs without approval

    Before the agent writes any code, it shows its plan: inputs, columns and steps. The scientist confirms or edits it, and every plan is kept in the Agent Plans tab, so each result can be traced back to its reasoning.

Data Merging — the agent proposes a merging plan
Anomalous Data Detection — options for each flagged issue
Analysis — insights, interpretation and next steps
  1. 03

    One workspace per job

    Everything the agent produces for a job lives in the side panel: assets, datasets, R code and plans. The hard part was scale. One job can produce many scripts and plans, and each carries required attributes: version, original or edited state, and a timestamp.

  2. 04

    Grouping instead of endless tabs

    Assets sit in a vertical rail sorted by type, with extra items collapsed into a counter. Code files are grouped by the kind of output they produce, each group with its own marker and count, so a dozen scripts read as a few groups. Any section can be expanded to full screen.

Deep dive 02

From many chats to one report

A real analysis rarely fits in one conversation: merging happens in one chat, cleaning in another, the final plots in a third. The old way of building reports was slow and had no AI help.

  1. 01

    One decision per step

    I split report generation into a wizard: Select Collections, Select Chats and Assets, Grouping Assets, Report Preview. The product is already dense, so each step asks for one decision and keeps everything else out of the way.

  2. 02

    Picking the right assets

    The hardest part was choosing assets across many chats. On the selection step, the chat stays visible next to its assets, so a scientist picks a chart while seeing how it was produced. Chosen items collect in a separate Report Assets column and can be removed at any time.

  3. 03

    A preview you can edit

    The last step is an editable preview of the generated report, with basic formatting, before it is exported.

Step 1 — select a collection and its chats
Step 2 — pick assets with the chat in view
Step 4 — editable report preview

More screens

Around the workspace

Sign-in, onboarding, variable mapping, file management and shared chats. In a later update I moved navigation to a deep navy sidebar: the accent color separates it from the workspace and keeps attention on the analysis. In a system this complex, every simplification counts.

Sign in
Welcome — choose a collection and datasets
Variable Map — match columns to analysis variables
File Manager — code and outputs by study
Chats — own and shared, grouped by project
